entry.title: Band To Watch: PISS

entry.content:
CONTENT WARNING: Sexual violence, sexual assault, and discussions of trauma.

When is art successful? That’s obviously meant to be a ridiculous rhetorical question. But Vancouver quartet PISS — vocalist/lyricist Taylor Zantingh, guitarist Tyler Patterson, bassist Gavin Moya, and drummer Garreth Roberts — and their debut album you made me / skin on linen, have got me thinking some big, ridiculous things. Why do a gnarled scream and grating guitars sound so good? Why do we turn pain into sound? Why do we feel pain? Why do we inflict pain? What do I get from seeing someone else’s pain? These are only a very minute fraction of the difficult questions that PISS’ music brings to mind. 

you made me / skin on linen stopped me in my tracks. It’s an assemblage of guttural yells, engrossing poetry, samples of feminist thinkers and activists, grueling bass, unyielding drums, and landmine guitars. In just over 30 minutes, the album articulates the evolution of personhood in a world that seems to welcome sexual violence, the societal norms that have allowed such violence to continue throughout history, and the oppositional viewpoints on how to move forward and prevent that injustice from continuing. 

Each sample feels like a doorway to some new level of both understanding and unraveling. The album opens with children's voices expressing what they want to be when they grow up. On the following track “i wanted to be a singer,” Zantingh relays one line about how everything, any idea of the future or who can be, changes based on another person's abhorrent actions: "I wanted to write romance novels/ Now I need perfect control over my victim narrative/ The story of a girl who was silent and powerless/ But it's cliche to write about being powerless as a girl." The album then shifts between recordings of different feminist voices: Andrea Dworkin on her argument of pornography as a human rights violation; Manon Garcia discussing the Gisèle Pelicot case and the vastness of sexual violence; Toni Morrison speaking on morality, self-forgiveness, and grace.   

PISS expose the different ways to deal with pain and injustice. It’s more than just noise. It’s violent sound about violence inflicted on a body, a person, a future, a life. It’s a piece that’s about contradiction and tension, and how life moves forward as a result of constant friction.

For two years, PISS performed the same set. Now, a version of it has become their debut album for Sub Pop. What began as a project built around a specific artistic vision has become part of a larger conversation about personal autonomy and systemic violence. It feels silly to write about such a standalone work, and I was reminded while chatting with the band over Zoom, just before they headed out on a nine-hour car ride for tour, that it’s also silly for me to request explanations for something that feels most powerful when experienced — whether live or blasted through headphones. One could argue that’s when art is most significant. 

Preview you made me / skin on linen below and read an edited version of our chat below.

Are you excited to go on tour? When was the last show or shows you guys played?

TAYLOR ZANTINGH: We did a weekend trip in Toronto, and we were supposed to play a festival in Windsor as well. Or not Windsor. Where was it? Kitchener, Ontario. Both in Canada. But I lost my voice at the first show, so I'm a little nervous. But I've been doing tons of vocal exercises and trying to stay on top of my health, not get sick. I love being on tour, but it's a constant state of hyper vigilance concerning — I'm always listening to everyone's breathing, like oh, someone's sniffling. If I hear someone cough, I'm just like, "Ahhhh!"

Your vocal athleticism is so fricking cool. I’m always in awe of people that can scream. It takes such stamina. So I'm curious to hear about your background and your journey to find your voice as a performer.

ZANTINGH: I never did any training or vocal training. I took singing lessons when I was a kid, but then very quickly my singing teacher was like, "Oh, we need to teach you guitar." So she was secretly teaching me guitar when I was supposed to be doing singing lessons. But I think for me, it's the journey to discover my voice is like it always felt natural for me to be loud. I guess very early on I was in my high school boyfriend's punk band when I was like 16 years old, and I was screaming back then, and I just really enjoyed it. In this band, all the years of not thinking too critically about things and letting myself reach a flow state on stage, coupled with all the really intense thinking I had been doing about words and lyrics when I was doing my undergraduate degree in creative writing, came together so that this project, my approach to voice is very intuitive. There's not a lot of thought that goes into delivery. The thought goes into everything else, so that I don't have to think that much about voice. 

But it has been a really interesting relationship with my body as an instrument in this project, because on one hand, my voice has allowed me to unlock this life for myself and express all these things and connect with all these people. It's a huge tool for empowerment for me, but it's also extremely humbling because when I lose my voice, it all just goes away. When I reach my limits, I think humbling is the only word I could use to describe it because I can't take my body to a shop and get it re-strung or you know whatever if my instrument breaks. The obsession with my voice, the obsession with my body, like vocal warm ups and vocal cool down exercises when we're off tour physiotherapy massage therapy, regular therapy, like taking care of my body. It's been a very interesting experience because the project is so much about my body too, right?

I was just thinking that it’s an interesting parallel of again this tension of the body versus the mind and how they're constantly battling each other, but also can be in harmony with each other at certain points. I'm in love with the record because it so eloquently talks about such difficult things, but at the same time. I love music that can feel like it's about to break, but at the same time is so strong and it's controlled chaos in a way. 

ZANTINGH: Oh, thank you. I really enjoyed when we were writing the record, and even the ongoing process of playing the set over and over again, thinking about the relationship between the music and myself as a character. You know what I mean? So when we were writing the record, it was thinking about the music as the environment in which I exist, telling my story. So that's why the music feels so violent sometimes. But when we're playing on stage, we put a lot of effort into making sure that the the music is dialed in, and even when we have technical difficulties, we do not stop a song unless it's absolutely necessary and keep going so that I can feel the security to not have to think when I'm performing, and I can get into that place that allows me to actually connect with people in a sort of... I don’t want to say spiritual, but you know what I mean, like connect with them in an energetic way.

Even when we're on stage, things have to feel safe enough for me that I can start to think about the instruments in real time as dangerous for me. There are times when we go on stage and I'll take my earplugs out for certain parts of the song, and it's very important to me to protect my ears because like I need them as a musician. But in certain moments, it just makes sense and feels right for me to do that because it's an important part of the set for people to watch me hurting — which sounds fucked up to say, but that's what people like about it, you know? 

This album has really made me think a lot about performance of a narrative and how people are supposed to receive art. One question that I had for everyone in the band was if there's art or albums that are so important but they're so difficult to listen to every day. There's this tension between recognizing something is really important and sacred, but also at the same time knowing that you need space from it, and it can't be something that's just purely enjoyable all the time.

ZANTINGH: Yeah, I think the closest thing that I could relate to people on that feeling is the record A Crow Looked At Me, which is the Mount Erie record about when his wife passed away. He does talk a lot in that record about refusing to let that experience become an object for somebody else in a way. Like he's making art about it, but he's really pissed off that he even has to. I think in that direct address of, hey, you're listening to this in the comfort of your bus seat on your way to your work, but this is like tearing apart my entire life. And when I first heard that record, I was just like, "holy fuck," because it does multiple things. It forces you to sit with him in a moment in a way that you wouldn't necessarily otherwise. You would think about your own life when you're listening to a song, but he's like, no, I am here, and that's what this record's about, and I think that sort of feeling really inspired me when I was making this record of refusing to let something be commodified in the way that art sometimes is. 

GAVIN MOYA: I don't know. I was also thinking about Mount Eerie, but I can't really think of another example. Maybe Carrie & Lowell, by Sufjan Stevens, is another one about grieving someone. It hurts to listen to in a way that is not for everyday listening. 

I would love to hear more about your experience in the tension maybe between releasing or exorcising these emotions and also putting it down in a creative aspect in order to contain it or maybe make sense of it, or maybe to put it outside of yourself. But then to also have to like again revisit that as a touring musician. 

ZANTINGH: Yeah, yeah. I mean, it's all of those things you said at one time sometimes. I think being in this project, I have learned to completely detach myself from any sort of expectation of what things should feel like or what I should be experiencing, and understand my role in this as a completely unique thing that is what it is in that moment. If that makes sense? There are times when we're driving and we've just had a big laugh because something is so funny and we're in a beautiful city and I'm looking out the window and I'm just so joyful and grateful, and then there are times when we're about to leave for tour and my knees have been hurting since the last tour and I'm worried about my voice, and I'm stressed out, and I'm crying myself to sleep because I don't want to go on tour. 

And there are times when I'm terrified because there's very strange parallels between the experience of getting on stage and telling a bunch of strangers this thing that happened to me, and what happened? What actually happened to me? And when I was trying to communicate my story and have people receive my experience and my truth, and the parallels between very valid art criticism and having your experience criticized or your story criticized — it's so many different things at once that you have to learn to get comfortable in a constant place of tension and to just let things go, let go of control. Which is very hard for people who have experienced trauma, [laughs] letting go of control, understanding that I can't control how people receive the project. I can't control how people talk about the project. I can't control how people perceive me, how they relate to me, what they say to me, what they do at my shows. 

The only thing that I’ve found that has started to make it easier for me is somatic therapy and learning to just sit in a feeling without constantly needing to be like, "Oh, what does this mean? What does this mean?" Because so many things have happened. There's a backlog where I'm still processing things in this experience that have happened to me months ago, and then there's new things being added to the queue, and it's hard to think about what's happening right now when there's still all this other stuff that's — what I'm trying to say in a very long-winded way is that it's an ongoing and organic, living, evolving process, and I have to see it that way in order to function.

I think that's really beautiful as well because it sounds you're inhabiting the project as well as interacting with the structure with which the project exists in. The idea of sound collage is really cool and super effective, and it feels like everything is constantly in conversation with each other. I wanted to know more about your relationship with collage and why you felt that that was an important way to structure the album.

ZANTINGH: Yeah, I really liked the idea of this assemblage as a metaphor for creating yourself and the way that like environment changes you or helps you or changes the way or influences the way that you grow, especially as a child, and I like the idea of assemblage/collage with literal objects and how that feels when you're using that as a device to talk about an experience within womanhood, especially. Then to further that, the idea of object and fragments and collage and assemblage when you're a performer, the other layer of a performer that exists as a different thing inside everyone's mind, but is constantly resisting like objectification while you're doing all that, I was attracted to that as something where the piece never has to be finished.

You say collage, but when I was writing the record, I was thinking of assemblage art, which is like a type of collage, right? That's just the word that I prefer to use. But it was one of those things where when I started thinking about how to talk about the things that I wanted to talk about without slipping into cliches, it made sense to work with as many different things as possible, an amalgamation of all the different things that influenced me and helped me and challenged me.

And that's why I think sometimes some people perceive the things as being in conflict because maybe they're newer to the conversation. They're not used to how two very influential feminist thinkers can be in direct conflict with each other, but yet both their ideas are essential for us to move forward as a movement, and at the same time for us to exist and have that duality within ourselves of we were deeply harmed and victims, but at the same time, we're capable of hurting others, perpetuating that harm, perpetuating harm upon ourselves, of being complicit in our own harm.

I think that constant contradiction and how we are made up of all these different things. I don't know. It's it's very hard for me to explain in words because, like, I made the record, right, because I don't know how to just say it in a sentence. If I could just be like, "Yeah, this is what the record's about, and this is everything," then I wouldn't have made the record because it would have just been something that's easy to describe. So I hope there's something in there that you can paraphrase and something that makes sense. But that's kind of where my head was at. 

From what I've read, it seems like sometimes the samples change within your live sets. Is that true?

ZANTINGH: The samples don't necessarily change in the live set, but they did change on the record because of legal issues. We ran into quite a few legal issues because when we started, we were just a little punk band, and we were like, Howard Stern is not going to care. But no, Howard Stern does care, and his team sent us a letter letting us know that he cares and that we absolutely cannot use his voice on our record. There were quite a few changes that had to be made on the record. So the samples that are on that record, most of them are the same as what we originally did, but there are three that changed because of legal issues. We couldn't clear or afford them. 

That's really interesting. Has that made you change your relationship with the album? 

ZANTINGH: Yeah. I had spent so long, and even before I was in the project, kind of saving YouTube videos of clips that I found particularly interesting or evocative, or that were kind of in the same conversation as the things that I liked to write about. I had continued to do that while we were making the record, and some of the samples that we ended up putting on the record were — well, one of them in particular, I had been saving for the next record, and the next record lives in the same universe as this one, obviously. So that sample in particular, sometimes I like to get frustrated, but we didn't have any time. It was literally like, "Oh, we have a week to clear this sample, and this one has a clear pathway to clear it, and it does make some sense on the record," but I find it a little bit underdeveloped personally, only because I know what I had planned originally to do with it in a second record.

I think it's a huge sore spot for me personally [laughs] because I had spent so long picking samples that I felt were perfect for the record, and then also the idea of the spectrum of responses to violence and the difference in ideological perspectives was really important to me. But we had somebody who elected not to be a part of the record because they thought — they were an estate manager for somebody else, and they thought this person was very staunchly nonviolent. And I wanted to include people who were all across the spectrum because I think that it's important for us to get really comfortable with discomfort, in order to progress as or progress as a movement.

She elected for her relative's voice to not be a part of it. But then, what ends up happening when you take the voice of those advocates for nonviolence out? Then it does start to skew more the other way. She didn't want to be involved in it because she didn't want to be involved in a project that was advocating for militant activism. But without your relative's voice, then it does really start to sound like it's advocating for militant activism. So I don't know. It's very complex how they all fit together like puzzle pieces in a way.

Yeah, that's so interesting. And again, it brings me back to that theme of everything is always in conversation with each other, whether you want it to be or not. Everything is ping-ponging off of each other, reacting, and so that’s interesting in a weird counteractive way, I guess, counterintuitive of what you were trying to do. 

ZANTINGH: Yeah, but I think that what we ended up with, it was as good as we could manage, considering the logistical hurdles that we had to overcome. And everybody else seems to think it's perfectly fine. I just know what I wanted to do and was unable to do that because of things that would not have affected us if we weren't in this awesome position of being signed to Sub Pop, using samples that you haven't cleared through.

You mentioned that you’re already thinking about writing the next record. I was curious what your conversations as a band have been like to creatively move forward when this started as a project that was really just to create one specific idea or one album? How do you move forward collaboratively as a group when that's been done?

ZANTINGH: We will only proceed the same way as we did with the first record, which we have been playing around with stuff sonically, which has been very exciting and personally inspiring. But subject matter-wise, we're all on the same page that, for me as a writer, I need a lot of peace and quiet and solitude in my life in order to make things that I think are actually interesting. I could sit down and write songs, but I'm not gonna like them, and they're not gonna be any good. So I think we're definitely not in a rush to make something. I think good things take time, and I'm not going to write something if I don't feel like it should be written, if that makes sense. I think we're just focusing on touring this record, and then trying to find a cutoff point where I can have a lot of space and go back to reading a lot and sitting with my thoughts and making a lot of bad stuff so that I can make good stuff after.

At this point in the conversation, the full band gathers on the couch post-coffee run.

When you guys first came together as a group, what was the thing that made you all think, "Okay, this is gonna work"? What was your first clicking conversation or touchstone?

ZANTINGH: I want to say when I made the document. 

TYLER PATERSON: Yes. Yeah. I don't know if Tay went over this already, but Tay and I met initially, and then after kind of bringing Garreth and Gavin into the band, Tay had created this outline of what this entire album was going to be, with a lot of abstract terms, being like, "Okay, this song is maybe conceptually this vibe, and this one who's giving this energy," and different prompts to jump off from. That was when everything got a little more solidly glued together. But also getting into the practice room the first few times, I feel like you kind of know in a band dynamic and setting very quickly whether things are going to be good or bad. I think very quickly we all gelled really well together. 

ROBERTS: Was the document made for the first time that we practiced?

ZANTINGH: Maybe with you, made before the first time we practiced with you, because it was over Halloween week when I went to go cat sit. And I was just alone for the week, and then we jammed for the first time in early November, right?

ROBERTS: Yeah. 

ZANTINGH: In the beginning, Ty and I were writing all the songs together, and the last three or four songs that we wrote, we wrote all as a big group. But that was after we had already started playing shows together. I think maybe also a moment where we were all like, "holy shit," was when we played our first show and we saw the reception that everybody — like, it was a modest crowd, not too many people, but I was really overwhelmed by how many people were talking after and their experience of the set.

ROBERTS: That show and then also the Music Waste one I think are the two big ones at the start.

What's something the other members have introduced you to musically or otherwise that has changed your perspective on art? 

ROBERTS: Whoa!

MOYA: This is an easy one for me. I never in my life would listen to noise music or [music] half as experimental as what Ty and Tay were wanting to cook up. When Ty sent me the playlist of what him and Tay were going for sonically, I'd never heard anything like it. I was like, "This is crazy." The first time we started jamming, Ty was like, "Bring every pedal you have." Immediately, I was like, "My god, I've never even thought in my life how to make sounds like this." And it was really, really exciting to just make disgusting noises that I didn't know were possible.

ROBERTS: I felt very similar, but then also I guess there's maybe specific artists too that I was just like, "Holy shite." Actually, really got into Women through because Ty and Tay are both big fans of Women and that was like a really really big one.

ZANTINGH: Women the band, Women the band. [Laughs].

I'll make sure to clarify that. 

ROBERTS: The gender, the social instruction. [Laughs]. That was maybe one of the bigger ones, but there's been a few for sure. But yeah, I didn't listen to any noise music or anything in that realm. 

PATERSON: For me, it was definitely going to Tay’s poetry reading. I think that was a really important moment because we had been writing in a more casual sense and jamming in my room before then, but I think that solidified at least an idea of a particular direction that we could really explore, and I feel like from that point, then the project just kind of exploded from there.

ZANTINGH: Ty's music taste is very broad, and I've discovered a lot of different artists that I wouldn’t normally listen to through being friends with him and collaborators with him. But also, it's been really exciting, especially in the early days. We just have extremely complementary skill sets where things that I have no idea how to even think about, and he would just be fluent in it, and then vice versa. I think it made it feel like learning in a fun way, rather than like, "Oh fuck, I have to learn this in order to make this song." I just have this artist who I respect so much, who is bringing all these things that I have been missing from my own practice, and I can just focus on doing what I do best, and doing that to the best of my abilities, and trust that this person who I've chosen to collaborate with is going to do the same on his end. That was exciting because it was the music language that he brought to the project that helped me unlock so much. Because I would just give him these weird abstract prompts, and then he would translate that into real sound. 

This is, I guess, kind of a spicy one. But what is the most unexpected thing you've disagreed about as a band?

ZANTINGH: I think maybe you guys could say that because the thing is that we have a pretty clear structure for decision making. Like they might disagree with something, but not even really tell me [laughs]. Because if I'm like, "Yeah, I really want to do this," then they're just gonna say their opinion — 

PATERSON: I can’t really think of anything off the top of my head. 

ROBERTS: I think any actual disagreements are going to be about just like pop culture or liking bands or something.

ZANTINGH: And when we were writing, Gary wanted to use a lot more toms. 

ROBERTS: Oh! 

[Everyone laughs].

PATERSON: You snuck some in there. 

ROBERTS: I did. I did. I don't even know if it was a disagreement though. 

MOYA: It was a disagreement or a severe misunderstanding. 

ZANTINGH: We were recording the last song on the record, and during the noise part, I had been listening to a demo over and over again where Gary did a specific thing with his drums during that part, and then he kept recording it, and I would go in and give notes and be like, "Oh, can you do this?" And he'd be like, "Yeah, yeah." But then he kept doing the other thing, so we had like a… fight in the studio. 

ROBERTS: I just remember it you basically were like, "You've done it before this way. Like, I want you to do exactly like how we had been practicing it," and how we had been practicing it had changed from when that demo was. So I was in my head how we've been practicing. It was a completely different thing from what you thought we’d been practicing was. And so I and I didn't even know. 

ZANTINGH: Gary and I have a Donkey/Shrek type relationship.

[Everyone laughs].

PATERSON: She did it.

ROBERTS: She did it. 

ZANTINGH: Any disagreements that happen are between us, but then also I would not be able to function in this band without him. But we do butt heads a lot, just personality wise, I think.

MOYA: Yeah, usually by accident.

ZANTINGH: We’re arguing, and then I'm like, "Wait, we're both on the same side. Hey, we agree."

ROBERTS: Fifteen minutes in, we’re like, "Okay, well, let's just keep going."

ZANTINGH: Yeah, yeah. But other than that, there's not a lot of disagreements. It's a very harmonious project, at least for me. 

ROBERTS: Yeah, I would agree.

How has making this album changed the way that you like to listen to music or experience art?

ZANTINGH: Yeah, it has definitely for me, but maybe not in ways that I expected. I noticed, for example, when we are on tour, we get to play shows with so many amazing bands and festivals, and for a long time I would be watching shows and be like, "Yes, this band is great," but feeling nothing. And then I went to a music festival just as a music fan, and I was watching this saxophonist called Jairus Sharif. He's from Calgary. He's playing in a church, and I was crying watching him. And then I went to see another Calgary band. This was Sled Island, so it's a Calgary music festival. I went to another Calgary band called Jed Arbor, and again, I was feeling so emotional, and I was like, "What the hell, do I like music?"

When I'm performing, I'm learning this now, but I have dissociated from my feelings consciously in order to get by. So it's been really hard to connect with art in the same way, only because we tour so much, and I live in a constant state of dissociation. So that's why I've been doing so much of somatic therapy and stuff like that to help me, because I want to feel all the things, but that's not always a conscious choice that you make. You have to work toward that.

PATERSON: Well, I was going to say the opposite. I think my approach to what I put into the project at the beginning and the songwriting process was kind of informed by the way that I'd been listening to music for a few years leading up to collaborating with the band, and in the sense where it was just searching for a little bit more and being a little bit more exploratory with the form of song and everything like that. That is what excited me at the beginning of this project, where you know Tay had this big document and outline for what the album could be, but there was a true freedom and of where we could pull sonically.

ROBERTS: I think being in a show environment so much, I would agree with Tay, how it just really affects how you experience it when you're then an audience member. I've been finding that I will go to shows, and in environments where I usually would like to really experience live music and be engaged with it, it's been harder to find those experiences. And it could just be from my music tastes changing, or really wanting to find performance and musicians that are doing something unique that affects me in a very specific way, or just from being constantly surrounded in that environment, that it sort of desensitized me to it. But I know that it can still happen though because I've been to shows this year that it's still been like, "Wow, yeah, it's not as common anymore."

PISS - you made me / skin on linen [LP]

Amazon(opens in new window)

you made me / skin on linen is out 10/30 via Sub Pop.

entry.title: Mei Semones – “2 Hands”
entry.summary: Hear "2 Hands," another beautiful song from genre-blurring Artist To Watch Mei Semones' forthcoming album 'Howl.'
entry.content:
We named Mei Semones an Artist To Watch last year on the strength of her debut album Animaru, an idiosyncratic yet seamlessly polished amalgamation of jazzy guitar, bossa nova rhythms, chamber-pop arrangements, and indie rock heft. She announced its follow-up Howl, her first for Verve/Interscope, and shared its lovely title track last month. And today she's back with a second single.

"2 Hands" is another gorgeous offering, incorporating South Asian tabla into Semones' hybridized genre stew as she professes her devotion to music itself. "I'll give you my two hands/ I'll give you my whole heart / Offer my life and it's still not enough/ This path that continues forever/ As long as I live know what I need to do," she sings in both Japanese and English.

The song features a music video featuring Semones playing alongside her longtime bandmates Ransom McCafferty, Noah Leong, Claudius Agrippa, and Noam Tanzer. "Everyone in my band is such an incredible musician and I feel so lucky and grateful to play with them, and that's what this song is about!" she says. "So for this video I wanted to capture what it's like to play music with them, and highlight how amazing and talented each of them are. Thank you to the director Jacob Rodier & the rest of the team for making us look cool." Watch and listen below.

Howl is out 1/15 on Verve/Interscope. Pre-order it here.

entry.title: Boys Noize – “Nächsteliebe” (Feat. Brutalismus 3000)
entry.summary: The veteran German dance producer Boys Noize recently spent a long time on the road with Nine Inch Nails, opening their shows and collaborating with them onstage, reworking some of their music to make it even clubbier than it already was. That experience led to the release of the fucking awesome collaborative album Nine Inch…
entry.content:
The veteran German dance producer Boys Noize recently spent a long time on the road with Nine Inch Nails, opening their shows and collaborating with them onstage, reworking some of their music to make it even clubbier than it already was. That experience led to the release of the fucking awesome collaborative album Nine Inch Noize earlier this year. Now, Boys Noize is getting ready to release 7LLVSION, his first solo album in five years, and his new single is a Brutalismus 3000 collab.

The German hardcore rave duo Brutalismus 3000 released their own album Harmony in June, and they collaborated with Boys Noize on lead single "I Bring My Gun To The Function." (We interviewed them when the KP came out.) Boys Noize and Brutalismus definitely make sense together, and their new single "Nächsteliebe" — German for "Love For One's Neighbor," apparently — is a harsh, hammering electro jam.

Boys Noize's 7LLVSION album also has tracks with Abra, TAICHU, Mayah Alkhateri, and others. Below, check out his videos for "Nächsteliebe" and lead single "1+1+1," featuring the Dutch rave artist ZEP.

7LLVSION is out 11/6 on Ones And Zeros.

entry.title: Beach House Drummer Graham Hill Announces Debut Solo Album Taking In Stars: Hear “Monster In My Head”
entry.summary: Last month, Beach House shared a Robert Lester Folsom cover for the 50th anniversary edition of Music And Dreams. Now, the dream-pop band’s drummer Graham Hill is announcing his debut solo album Taking In Stars. The twangy lead single “Monster In My Head” is here today. “I wrote this song after having a late night…
entry.content:
Last month, Beach House shared a Robert Lester Folsom cover for the 50th anniversary edition of Music And Dreams. Now, the dream-pop band's drummer Graham Hill is announcing his debut solo album Taking In Stars. The twangy lead single "Monster In My Head" is here today.

"I wrote this song after having a late night conversation with my son when he was having trouble falling asleep consistently as he was hitting his teenage years," Hill explains. "The line 'When I hear the smallest thing, and it snowballs into a scream' was pretty much verbatim how he described the issue to me. His particular experience was music playing repeatedly that he couldn't stop. It really resonated with me, as someone who has an active mind and sometimes obsessive tendency to overthink, especially when there are unresolved or uncertain things playing out in my current day-to-day reality."

Taking In Stars was co-produced with Donald Markowitz (Van Morrison, Taj Mahal) and features Shane Theriot (Neville Brothers, Willie Nelson), Gabe Stillman (Buddy Guy, ZZ Top), and more. Hear "Monster In My Head" below.

entry.title: Bryan Adams Drops Another Trump Diss Track And This One Mentions The Epstein Files
entry.summary: Canadian singer-songwriter Bryan Adams has shared a new diss track rebuking Donald Trump's efforts to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America."
entry.content:
Bryan Adams loves Canada and has, shall we say, somewhat less positive feelings towards Donald Trump. The Canadian singer-songwriter, an Ontario native, has not one but two Trump diss tracks on his forthcoming album How's It Goin'. The first, "51st State," was a rebuke to Trump's efforts to annex Canada into the United States of America that Adams decided to release on Canada Day, naturally. The second, which Adams shared yesterday, is called "Lake Ontario."

Trump has, for some reason, become obsessed with renaming bodies of water. Last year, he signed an executive order changing the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America." Earlier this year, he followed that up with another executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America." More recently, he's even floated the idea of renaming the Atlantic Ocean the "American Ocean" or "Trump Ocean," although Google apparently pushed back on that one. Bryan Adams is pushing back too, through the medium of song.

"Empires and regimes, dictators and kings, they all come and go. Lake Ontario is forever," Adams says in an statement. "This is a song for all the sane people on both shores who know that the current madness will pass, and that Lake Ontario will always be Lake Ontario." Here's a sample of the lyrics:

From glacial erosion - to indigenous care
From European exploration - to industrial wear and tear
The “lake of shining waters” is what the Iroquois called her
It’s a first nations name - not an executive order

But things weren’t going his way in Iran
So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram
He may have thought it best to throw a low blow
And create a real dog and pony show
But it feels like another distraction
While the Epstein files were getting traction
One day they’ll come out and we’ll say “there you go”
And then we’ll all dive into Lake Ontario

After centuries of trade and war
People settled down on the banks and shores
All rivalries and conflicts - had all but ceased
But it just took one dude to break that peace

Listen to "Lake Ontario" below.

How’s It Goin’ is out 11/6 via BAD.

entry.content:
IShowSpeed is a 21-year-old Cincinnati native who happens to be the most famous streamer on the planet. Millions of followers tune in to watch him get mobbed by fans across the planet while doing acrobatic flips and shouting hyped-up inspirational speeches. He also makes music sometimes, and he has one gold record, the 2026 single "World Cup." Frost Children are New York siblings who make glitchy, maximalist hyperpop. They have zero gold records. Recently, Speed made a quick burst of music with Frost Children while in the middle of a livestream.

I have no idea how this kind of thing happens, but Frost Children were part of an IShowSpeed livestreaming session in New York yesterday. Outside of their studio, Frost Children said, "We're making some dubstep" and invited Speed to make some music with them. Speed seemed confused by the term "dubstep" — I think he thought it was a dance style — and Frost Children hilariously locked themselves out of their studio for a long and excruciating moment while Speed posed for a photo with a little girl. Speed also told them, "Y'all look interesting." It's true! They do!

Once they finally got inside, Frost Children immediately hit play on a hyperactive track, and Speed danced for a few seconds, grabbed a mic, and did a bit of freestyling before grabbing a warm Red Bull on the way out. He was in Frost Children's studio for something like two and a half minutes, but I guess that counts as a collaboration. Watch it all happen below.

entry.title: Merry Halloween: A Scarily Early Guide To This Year’s New Christmas Albums
entry.summary: The spookiest part of spooky season?
entry.content:
It happens every year: Before spooky season even really gets rolling, musical artists start announcing new Christmas albums. If you're the type of person who despises Christmas music, the early onset yuletide onslaught might fill you with terror, which makes it a perfectly perverse annual Halloween-week feature here at Stereogum. Here is this year's potentially frightening holiday rundown.

Sufjan Stevens' Worst Chrismas Ever!

Let's start with the album Stereogum's indie-leaning listeners are most likely to care about. The new comp Worst Christmas Ever! brings together the best of Sufjan Stevens' myriad Christmas releases onto one disc. The 16-song tracklist includes one new song, "On This Christmas (It Only Gets Better)." It's Stevens' first new holiday tune in 15 years and first new song of any kind since recovering from Guillain-Barré syndrome. [Out 11/6 on Asthmatic Kitty.]

Alanis Morissette's Good Weather For Immaculate Conception

For several years now, Alanis Morissette has been releasing new holiday songs every time the season rolls around. Her first Christmas album, the cheekily titled Good Weather For Immaculate Conception, combines those tracks with new recordings. Guests include 2/3 of the Only Murders In The Building cast (sorry Selenators, it's Steve Martin and Martin Short), Brandi Carlile, Joy Oladokun, Amythyst Kiah, and Trans Voices. Morissette teased the album with a version of the bluegrass Christmas traditional "Beautiful Star Of Bethlehem" featuring Carlile and banjo enthusiast Martin. [Out 11/6 on Epiphany Music.]

The Cast Of The Gilded Age's Voices Of The Gilded Age: The Christmas Album

Here's what I know about HBO's The Gilded Age: It's set in 1880s New York City, it was created by Downtown Abbey's Julian Fellowes, and the GOAT Carrie Coon is in it. The show is not a musical, but its cast is full of Broadway veterans, and apparently some fans have clamored for a musical episode. The next best thing: a Christmas album on which the actors perform a slew of holiday standards, plus two new tunes composed by veteran hitmaker Desmond Child. Coon plus castmates Ben Ahlers, Christine Baranski, Laura Benanti, Denée Benton, Jordan Donica, Celia Keenan-Bolger, Audra McDonald, Brian Stokes Mitchell, Donna Murphy, Kelli O’Hara, Taylor Richardson, Morgan Spector, Taylor Trensch, and Adrienne Warren all sing on the album, and the results sound way more 20th century than 19th century to me. [Out 11/6 via Concord Theatricals.]

Niia's Christmas With Niia

Alt-R&B singer Niia's new Christmas With Niia is a new entry in the canon of jazzy, self-consciously "cozy" Christmas albums. She worked on it with producer Spencer Zahn, which should immediately perk your ears up. The lead single was a cover of Paul McCartney's divisive "Wonderful Christmastime" that replaces the original version's playful quirkiness with a wistful smoothness that's really working for me. This one might end up in my holiday rotation. [Out digitally 10/30 and physically 12/4 via Candid Records.]

Ryan Peter Murphy's Christmas In New England

There will always be a market for Michael Bublé types. Ryan Peter Murphy is a 24-year-old Connecticut-born Berklee student who bills himself as a "swooner" ("Gen Z’s answer to the crooner," explains a press release). That makes him a prime candidate to record a Christmas album, and so he has. Unlike fellow young traditionalist Laufey, Murphy is not putting any kind of nouveau twist on his trad-pop pastiches. Songs from his new Christmas In New England are even being featured in the new crop of Hallmark Channel Christmas movies this year, so I'd guess his appeal is multi-generational. The only modern aspect of Christmas In New England's title track is an animated video that looks like AI. [Out now on Warner.]

aron!'s christmas dream EP

There's more than one of these young crooner guys. You can tell aron! is Gen Z because he insists upon lowercase branding, but like Ryan Peter Murphy, his self-described "cozy pop" (yes, this kid keeps it cozy all year long) is all the way retro. That means he, too, is ideally suited for a project like the forthcoming christmas dream EP. He delivers the snappy big band single "Christmas Dreams" with a surprisingly casual swagger. [Out 11/13 via Verve.]

Hilary Duff's Holiday Things EP

Famous millennial mom and resurgent Ladder spokesperson Hilary Duff got into the Christmas music game with this month's Holiday Things EP, a mix of three originals and two covers that strikes me as one of the best pop yuletide efforts since Ariana Grande's Christmas & Chill. It opens with the brilliantly titled "All You Want For Christmas Is Me." [Out now via Sugarmouse/Atlantic.]

Steven Page's Steven's Greetings

In 2004, when Steven Page was still in the Barenaked Ladies, he and his bandmates released a Christmas album called Barenaked For The Holidays. He left the band in 2009, and after years of solo releases, he's made his way back to yuletide fare. Next month's Steven's Greetings features a mix of originals and standards, including a few of the songs he sang on Barenaked For The Holidays. There are a couple Hanukkah tunes mixed in too. The album spans the jokey-to-heartfelt emotional range we've come to expect from this guy; it begins with Page passionately singing "I'm gonna make a cheese log with cream cheese and cheddar cheese" and ends with a straight-faced rendition of "Auld Lang Syne" featuring his three adult sons. [Out 11/13 via Fresh Baked Goods.]

The Infamous Stringdusters' Dust The Halls Vol. 2

Progressive bluegrass mainstays the Infamous Stringdusters put out Dust The Halls: An Acoustic Christmas Holiday! back in 2020. The sequel, Dust The Halls Vol. 2, puts a rustic spin on the expected mix of hymns, standards, and originals. [Out 11/13 via Americana Vibes.]

Kat Edmonson's Have Your Merry Christmas With Me

Jazz-pop singer Kat Edmonson is no stranger to holiday music. She appeared on Lyle Lovett's Songs For The Season in 2011 and released her own Holiday Swingin'! (A Kat Edmonson Christmas, Vol. 1) in 2021. Now comes another similar offering, Have Your Merry Christmas With Me. Based on advance singles "It's Snowing" and "That's What I Want For Christmas," the originals will successfully capture the jazzy traditional essence of the covers. [Out 11/6 via self-release.]

Debbie Gibson's Winterlicious D’Luxe

Former teen idol Debbie Gibson successfully ventured into the holiday realm with 2022's Winterlicious. Ahead of a Christmas-themed Las Vegas residency this December, she recently dropped a deluxe edition of the album with six new tracks including "Lit Up," a single that reminds me this woman paved the way for Britney Spears. [Out now via Stargirl.]

David Benoit's David Benoit Conducts A Vince Guaraldi Holiday Symphony

I don't know why you would listen to Vince Guaraldi covers when the originals are right there, but if you're looking for a fresh spin on Guaraldi's timeless material from A Charlie Brown Christmas, David Benoit has got you covered. The jazz pianist and composer worked with the Czech National Symphony Orchestra on David Benoit Conducts A Vince Guaraldi Holiday Symphony. On lead single "Christmas Time Is Here," they get an assist from the All-American Boys Choir. [Out digitally 10/30 and physically 11/20 via Candid.]

Norah Jones & Chris Stapleton's “April’s Gone"

As Christmas trifles go, you could do a lot worse than a rootsy one-off single from Norah Jones and Chris Stapleton. Jones wrote "April's Gone" with Leon Michels of El Michels Affair, who produced her 2021 holiday album I Dream Of Christmas and 2024's Visions. The new track isn't going to end these performers' reputation as Starbucks music, but it would sound great at a coffee shop.

Johan Agebjörn & Dana Jean Phoenix - "Will You Be Home For Christmas"

On the new single "Will You Be Home For Christmas," Swedish producer Johan Agebjörn and synthwave singer-songwriter Dana Jean Phoenix dare to imagine a Drive soundtrack version of Christmas music. It ends up somewhere a bit chintzier than that, but good try! [Out 11/27 via self-release.]

entry.title: Hasan Piker Explains Damon Albarn Meetup At Gorillaz Show
entry.summary: On Sunday, the left-wing streamer and activist Hasan Piker tweeted the above photo of himself with “the legend damon albarn,” at a Los Angeles Gorillaz show. Apparently, some Gorillaz fans were surprised and/or upset at the connection. (The Democratic Party has invested tons of resources into depicting the pro-Palestine Piker as a kind of demonic…
entry.content:
On Sunday, the left-wing streamer and activist Hasan Piker tweeted the above photo of himself with "the legend damon albarn," at a Los Angeles Gorillaz show. Apparently, some Gorillaz fans were surprised and/or upset at the connection. (The Democratic Party has invested tons of resources into depicting the pro-Palestine Piker as a kind of demonic antisemitic figure.) As it turns out, though, Albarn first met Piker almost two years ago, when he and his daughter Missy attended a Piker lecture in Oxford.

Albarn's daughter is apparently a Piker fan, and an Albarn fan Instagram has a clip of Piker talking about meeting Albarn after his Oxford speech. (That might be Piker's last time in the UK for a while; his visa was revoked before a planned SXSW London appearance earlier this year.) The Instagram post also includes got a more recent clip of Piker talking about how Albarn invited him to see Gorillaz in LA, describing Albarn as a "pretty radical guy" and a "friend of the show, friend of the working class, friend of the revolutionaries all around." Piker says the show was "amazing."

Piker went to the Gorillaz show with fellow streamers Will Neff and Caroline Kwan, and they all met up with Albarn and Gorillaz co-founder Jamie Hewlett backstage.

Less controversially, Albarn also met Wes Eisold from Cold Cave and American Nightmare.

Also, Tony Hawk met Del The Funky Homosapien and De La Soul's Posdnous in that same star-studded Forum backstage area.

According to Setlist.fm, that night's Gorillaz show included a couple of tour debuts, live rarities like "Pac-Man," a rare Jamie Hewlett stage appearance, and surprise guests like ScHoolboy Q, on the live rarity "Pac-Man," and Kali Uchis, on the 2017 Gorillaz song "She's My Collar." Onstage, it looked like Albarn politely declined an invitation to grind with Uchis.

Gorillaz and Kali Uchis previously shared the stage a few times in 2017, and Albarn appeared on Uchis' 2018 song "In My Dreams." Uchis' posts after the show led fans to speculate that they're working on another collaboration.

entry.title: Sphere Coming To Maryland
entry.summary: More Spheres are on the way. James Dolan’s insanely expensive, absurdly flashy Las Vegas venue has been operating since 2023, and Dolan’s Sphere Entertainment Company has plans to open more Spheres elsewhere in the world. As previously reported, an Abu Dhabi Sphere is expected to open in 2029, while London mayor Sadiq Khan rejected a…
entry.content:
More Spheres are on the way. James Dolan's insanely expensive, absurdly flashy Las Vegas venue has been operating since 2023, and Dolan's Sphere Entertainment Company has plans to open more Spheres elsewhere in the world. As previously reported, an Abu Dhabi Sphere is expected to open in 2029, while London mayor Sadiq Khan rejected a proposal to build another one in the city's Olympic Park. Now, it looks like the beautiful state of Maryland is about to get a smaller Sphere of its own.

Maryland Matters reports that the Prince George’s County Council has given the final approval to help publicly fund the construction of a smaller Sphere entertainment complex in National Harbor, right across the river from Washington, DC. On Tuesday, the eight-member Council voted unanimously to approve a deal that'll commit up to $215 million of county taxpayer money to the construction of a $1.4 billion Sphere complex. Under that plan, Sphere Entertainment will gradually pay the county back for its investment.

While the Las Vegas Sphere seats 17,600 concertgoers, the proposed National Harbor Sphere will only have 6,000 seats. When they presented the proposal, reps for the Sphere Entertainment Co. said that they hoped the venue would be open for shows as early as 2030.

The deal with the the Prince George’s County Council includes labor union agreements, though they're reportedly not as strong as many union workers hoped. County Executive Aisha Braveboy tells Maryland Matters, "This project is projected to generate $63 million annually in just property tax and sales and amusement tax alone." She claims that it'll more than offset the loss of the Washington Commanders, who are about to return to their old home of Largo, and the recently closed Six Flags America amusement park.

National Harbor is a planned resort-type area that's full of antiseptic-looking bars. It has been developed quickly over the last 15 years or so, and its current visual signature is the Capital Wheel, a giant neon-lit Ferris wheel. There's an MGM casino there, too. The place has a real corporate-entertainment vibe, so this Sphere should fit right in.

As it happens, I was just in National Harbor on Saturday, and I am in no hurry to return. After the giant free Turnstile show in DC, I went up a tall-people meetup at a National Harbor bar. Driving into that place was a nightmare, so if you're going to this hypothetical future Sphere, you should plan public-transportation options way in advance. The bar was crowded as hell, and the cologne/perfume smell was overpowering, but it was cool to be in a room full of people my height. Look at this shit!

Glorious. But unless there are further Tall Tour events at the National Harbor Sphere, I'll probably stay away. What is this thing going to 495 traffic, anyway? Can the Beltway possibly get worse?

entry.content:
In 2024, Flower Face's sprawling fourth album Girl Prometheus earned her our Artist To Watch honor. Now, Ruby McKinnon is announcing its followup Kill The Muse, arriving next year. Stereogum is presenting her sold-out show at Brooklyn's Public Records one week from today on Thursday, Nov. 5.

The new single "Better The Devil" is out now, following August's "Bad Dream." "I remember so vividly the moment I wrote this song," the Montreal musician says of "Better The Devil." She expands:

I was walking home from the metro station after spending the day at my producer Marcus’s studio working on the finishing touches of my last album. I was living alone, and I had spent the better part of the last year isolating myself as much as possible (when I wasn’t partying or pursuing awful, destructive relationships). My friends had all started a sobriety kick on January 1st, which I wasn’t inclined to join. It was the dead of winter, the worst time of year, when the sun sets at 4 PM, and I spent most evenings counting down the minutes until I could go to sleep. That night a friend was supposed to stay over, but she canceled, and I knew it was because she was pursuing her own awful, destructive on-and-off relationship. Everything felt so bleak. I got home with my nose running and my hands numb and sat down in the dark in my studio and wrote this song… It’s hard for me to listen to this song, even now. I feel so sad for that small, scared, trapped person that I was. I couldn’t see a way out. We saved some parts of that original demo I recorded in the moment, because they were so raw, painful, and unflinching. It felt like the first time I was really reckoning with myself and the downward freefall I had found myself in. Really, it felt like the first time I was being fully honest in a song.

Check it out below.

entry.title: Justice – “Pusher” (Feat. Gesaffelstein)
entry.summary: Justice team up with Gesaffelstein for "Pusher," a new track from their forthcoming 'Grand Theft Auto VI' score.
entry.content:
Grand Theft Auto VI is going to be an absolutely massive video game, and that video game is going to have an equally massive soundtrack. In addition to Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, a star-studded 34-track companion album featuring the likes of Cardi B, Travis Scott, Keith Richards, Yung Lean, Future, and PinkPantheress, there's an entirely separate 50-track Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score album from French blog-house overlords Justice.

"The scope of the game is so large geographically and thematically that it was clear from the beginning the music would also have to be very broad in terms of emotions, genres, and textures,” Justice's Xavier de Rosnay says. "We were given the freedom to explore as many things as we needed to, musically speaking."

We've already heard Justice's Tame Impala/SZA/King Gizzard-featuring, Dire Straits-aping synth-rock anthem "Flower In A Hurricane," which will apparently be included on both GTA VI albums. (It's also worth noting that it debuted at #62 on the Billboard charts, giving King Gizzard their first Hot 100 hit). And now we're getting "Pusher," an ominously throbbing seven-minute collab between Justice and French dance producer Gesaffelstein that sounds like it will go hard as hell while driving around Miami — sorry, Vice City — committing crimes. Hear it below.

Grand Theft Auto VI is out 11/19, and Justice's Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score album will be out 12/11 via Take-Two Interactive/Ed Banger/Because Music.

entry.title: Junior Boys Announce New Album The Gore: Hear “Underneath The Moon”
entry.summary: Junior Boys have announced the new album 'The Gore' and shared its
entry.content:
The Junior Boys are back in town. The Canadian electronic pop duo of Jeremy Greenspan and Matt Didemus are returning in February with The Gore, a follow-up and companion album to 2022's Waiting Game that Greenspan describes as "a polarized articulation of the same thing." Born out of a period of grief and loss following the deaths of Greenspan's father and a close friend from his youth and shaped by a nostalgia for horror, sci-fi, and experimental film, The Gore was conceptualized as a deliberately noisier, messier record.

"What if you made an album like Fresh by Sly and the Family Stone, or Here, My Dear by Marvin Gaye — messy records — but with the sonic language of Pan Sonic," Green explains in a statement. "Of course, I'm not good at translating that idea into something that actually sounds like that. Which, to be honest, has been a great asset — if I were able to faithfully rip off everything I wanted to rip off, I'd just sound like a ripoff."

Along with the announcement, the Boys are sharing the enigmatically burbling and echoing lead single "Underneath The Moon." According to Greenspan, "This song is deeply inspired by the 2022 horror film Skinamarink. I used old tape loop techniques using an old Tascam tape machine to achieve a number of the effects in the film, to work as a sort of homage to the ephemeral quality of analog recording tech." Hear it below.

entry.title: New York City Cops Shut Down Haywire’s Times Square Pop-Up
entry.summary: Boston hardcore band Haywire became underground heroes by playing endless numbers of wild live shows. They maintain an insanely busy touring schedule, and they’ve also got a habit of playing guerrilla-style sets in places where bands don’t usually play, or jumping on smaller regional shows at the last minute. But when Haywire tried to play…
entry.content:
Boston hardcore band Haywire became underground heroes by playing endless numbers of wild live shows. They maintain an insanely busy touring schedule, and they've also got a habit of playing guerrilla-style sets in places where bands don't usually play, or jumping on smaller regional shows at the last minute. But when Haywire tried to play a pop-up set in the middle of Times Square, the NYPD wasn't having it.

Earlier this month, Haywire released I Don't Wanna Say Goodbye, their second album and their first for bigger label Roadrunner. They've already made crazy videos for the singles "Interstate Love Affair" and "Sincerely Yours," and their Times Square set was supposed to be a shoot for another video. The band reportedly announced the set on Instagram story just an hour before it was supposed to take place on Wednesday night, posting a photo of the location and its longitude and latitude coordinates. A few hundred fans and friends showed up for some mosh madness, but the band only played a song and a half before police stormed in and shut everything down.

Per Setlist.fm, Haywire got through a performance of the I Don't Wanna Say Goodbye track "Flex Your Head," then launched into the anthemic singalong that's just called "Haywire." During that song, police stormed in, shoving moshers around and forcing them to disperse. One cop took the sticks right out of the drummer's hands. They took the amps, too! But Haywire's publicist tells us that there were no arrests, thankfully.

The happy irony, of course, is that Haywire probably got much better footage from that than they would've had if cops just let them finish what would've almost certainly been an extremely brief set. I'm sure that was not the most disruptive thing happening in Times Square at that exact moment. You can see the footage for yourself below.

I Don't Wanna Say Goodbye is out now on Roadrunner. Next month, Haywire will hit a couple of US festivals before heading off on an Australian tour.

entry.content:
Over the past few months, there's been a great deal of speculation about why longtime rhythm guitarist Nick Valensi decided to take a "temporary break" from the Strokes. Valensi played on the Strokes' new album Reality Awaits, and his most recent performance with the band was at Coachella in April. Last year, Strokes frontman Julian Casablancas mentioned that he no longer speaks with Valensi. But right now, speculation is all we have. The Strokes are touring without Valensi, and Valensi sometimes pops up onstage with other rock stars.

On Wednesday night, the Strokes played Dublin, with Longwave's Steve Schlitz filling in for Valensi, as he's done for the past few months. Valensi, meanwhile, was over in Paris, joining a different band onstage. Last month, Valensi joined Strokes contemporary Jack White at an LA show. And last night, Valensi popped up onstage when Duran Duran played Accor Arena.

Duran Duran are not exactly Strokes contemporaries, but Nick Valensi does have a connection to the band. Valensi is married to the photographer and TV presenter Amanda de Cadenet, who was previously married to Duran Duran bassist John Taylor. Duran Duran closed out their Paris show with their 1982 smash "Rio," and Valensi joined them. But there was some kind of technical issue with Valensi's guitar, so the show pretty much stopped for a few minutes while Simon Le Bon attempted to riff and stagehands tried to get Valensi's guitar working. You can see it happen below.

entry.title: DIIV – “Dare Me”
entry.summary: DIIV's new A. G. Cook-produced record ZIRP! is officially out on Friday. Hear the new single "Dare Me" and watch its music video.
entry.content:
DIIV's new A. G. Cook-produced record ZIRP!, which just so happens to be our reigning Album Of The Week, is officially out on Friday. We've already heard early tracks "The Fountain," "Kid," and "Trillions," two of which made it onto our hallowed 5 Best Songs Of The Week lists. Today, we're getting one final single before the drop, "Dare Me," which continues fusing their shoegaze sensibilities with squiggly electronic textures. It also comes with an atmospheric music video, directed by Louie Kovatch, in which the band performs the song in an abandoned office while clad in the rumpled businesswear they've been sporting lately. Watch and listen below.

DIIV have several festival appearances in Europe coming up, and they've also announced a huge world tour kicking off in Australia in February and concluding in the UK in the end of June.

entry.title: Queens Of The Stone Age – “Run Away From The Mob”
entry.summary: Queens Of The Stone Age are releasing their new album 'Perfecth' on Friday, and today they're sharing closing track "Run Away From The Mob."
entry.content:
Queens Of The Stone Age are releasing their new album, the slightly infuriatingly titled Perfecth, on Friday. The last single from the record found newly minted silver fox Josh Homme wondering "Where The Goth Girls At?" Today, we're getting closing track "Run Away From The Mob," which originally dates back to the session for 2013's ...Like Clockwork and features Dave Grohl behind the drum kit.

"It's a letter, a last one, addressed to an oldest son," Homme explains. "'If you're reading this, everything went wrong, and here’s what you have to do.' The end is the sound of a father standing behind his son." An examination of mob mentality and the court of public opinion, the song builds from a mournful guitar figure to an explosive expression of unconditional loyalty. Listen below.

Perfecth is out 10/30 on Matador.

entry.title: Jim James Announces Memoir
entry.summary: Over the summer, Jim James released Wowed Out, his first solo album in eight years. Now, the My Morning Jacket frontman is announcing a memoir titled One Wonders. It hits the shelves next spring. The book, which is his first, follows his Louisville upbringing, his love for music, and his struggles with depression and drinking.…
entry.content:
Over the summer, Jim James released Wowed Out, his first solo album in eight years. Now, the My Morning Jacket frontman is announcing a memoir titled One Wonders. It hits the shelves next spring.

The book, which is his first, follows his Louisville upbringing, his love for music, and his struggles with depression and drinking. In a statement, he wrote, "If nothing else, I hope the main thing someone takes away from this book (aside from learning more about the joys and challenges of being a working artist and musician) is that it’s okay to ask for help. Everyone is going through some sort of challenge in this crazy world. IT IS POSSIBLE to find your way out of darkness and despair, and begin to enjoy the subtle, beautiful, everyday victories of simply being alive."

Read the full statement below.

Hello, friends! I am releasing a memoir!

Why? Why write this book? Why now?

As I’ve made good progress in therapy over the last five or six years, I’ve been doing a lot of reflecting on finding my voice — both as a singer, songwriter and musician, and as a person wandering the earth wondering…

what do I really want to SAY with my life overall?

As I reflect on my own musical journey (from first learning to play the guitar to creating music in the present day) and navigating the complexities of life in general, I have been thinking a lot about my elders. For so many of them, tradition was to never speak about yourself. You carried your victories and failures, your joys and horrors, quietly.

A thought kept making its way into my mind: wouldn’t things be lighter for all of us if we shared more with other people?

I feel like it’s our generation’s job to tear down those walls and share our triumphs and horrors.

When we do, we’ll find that we’re all walking around with the same things inside of us, the good and the bad.

It helps so much when we can find a way to let them out together, so that we can all begin to move toward a more peaceful and love-centered existence.

As if it WANTED this to happen and was WILLING it to happen, the Universe stepped in and began to line up the things I needed to write this book, bring it to life, and ACTUALLY PUBLISH it. And I began to realize its purpose:

Perhaps if I illustrated my journey, and how I began to deal with my own struggles with mental health, it could help people take a step toward getting out of their own darkness and depression.

If nothing else, I hope the main thing someone takes away from this book (aside from learning more about the joys and challenges of being a working artist and musician) is that it’s okay to ask for help. Everyone is going through some sort of challenge in this crazy world. IT IS POSSIBLE to find your way out of darkness and despair, and begin to enjoy the subtle, beautiful, everyday victories of simply being alive.

One Wonders will be available April 13, 2027 in hardcover and ebook, and as an audiobook, which I'll be reading. Additionally, Carmichael's Bookstore in Louisville will have autographed copies that you can preorder now.

One Wonders is out 4/13/27. Pre-order it here.
